idiom_name: sealed interface + kotlinx.serialization class discriminator + exhaustive when
implementation_notes: Kotlin's local idiom replaces both halves of the classic structure: a `sealed interface Command` gives a closed, compiler-registered hierarchy, and kotlinx.serialization writes the type discriminator itself (property `type` by default, configurable with `Json { classDiscriminator = ... }`, with @SerialName giving stable wire names), so the invoker needs no factory or registry - a `when` over the sealed type is exhaustive and compile-checked. If commands must be pluggable from other modules the hierarchy must become open: register each subtype in a SerializersModule and serialise through the base type. The classic base-class-plus-registry structure is justified mainly at Java-interop boundaries.
pitfalls: The discriminator value defaults to the fully-qualified class name: renaming or moving a command breaks old messages unless every type carries an explicit @SerialName, and changing the classDiscriminator property name invalidates messages already in the queue.

Sealed hierarchies are closed at compile time: a command added in another module cannot be deserialised through the base type without a SerializersModule, so "add a command without touching the invoker" holds only inside the same module set.
Unknown types throw SerializationException by default, and defaults/optional fields need encodeDefaults set consistently on both sides - a mismatch silently drops fields on the wire.
